query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: High-temperature processing of high-entropy alloys promotes the in situ formation of a dense, spinel-type oxide film enriched in elements like Al and Fe that simultaneously serves as a diffusion barrier to corrosive ions and a high-hardness, wear-resistant layer, thereby reducing the rate of degradation under combined corrosive and mechanical wear conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanocrystalline BCC solid-solution precursor powders prepared via mechanical alloying.
generation.intervention: Varying the sintering temperature (e.g., comparing processing at 1000 °C versus 850–950 °C) to induce or prevent robust passive film formation.
generation.conditions: Exposing alloy samples to a corrosive environment (3.5 wt% NaCl solution) paired with controlled wear (using a tribometer for abrasive/mechanical stress) under identical density and load conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, dense, spinel-type oxide film enriched in Al and Fe.
generation.mechanism: High-temperature sintering leads to surface elemental enrichment and subsequent formation of a protective oxide layer that limits the diffusion of corrosive species and resists mechanical removal due to its high hardness. This dual-action mechanism reduces the effective active surface area for corrosion and minimizes material loss from wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to lower-temperature sintered alloys, the high-temperature (1000 °C) processed alloy will exhibit a lower corrosion current density, higher charge transfer (or passive film) resistance, and reduced wear scar volume. Under simultaneous wear and corrosion, the degradation will be synergistically reduced compared to the sum of the individual effects observed in the baseline.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloys sintered at lower temperatures (850–950 °C) that form only a less robust passive film and show a predominant direct-attack corrosion mode with inferior wear resistance.
generation.boundary: This prediction should hold in environments where oxygen is available to support oxide film formation and under moderate abrasive conditions. It may fail in extremely abrasive environments that mechanically remove the oxide film faster than it can protect the substrate or in oxygen-starved conditions where film formation is suppressed.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative synergy between the wear and corrosion resistances and the detailed interaction of film degradation under simultaneous loading remain uncertain and will require further calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical high-entropy alloy samples, one sintered at a high temperature (1000 °C) to promote oxide film formation and the other at a lower temperature (850–950 °C) serving as the baseline. Subject both sets to a simultaneous degradation test using a corrosion cell with 3.5 wt% NaCl solution while applying a controlled mechanical wear load via a tribometer. Monitor the degradation until steady state is reached.
measurements: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to assess film resistance and charge transfer resistance.
Potentiodynamic polarization to obtain corrosion current densities and potentials.
Wear scar volume and depth measurements using profilometry or microscopy.
Microhardness tests and SEM/EDS analysis of surface morphology before and after testing.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-temperature (1000 °C) processed samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in both corrosion current density and wear scar volume relative to the lower-temperature samples (or if the robust oxide film is not maintained under mechanical load conditions), then the hypothesis is falsified.

System: MgAlTiVFeCo lightweight high-entropy alloy (designated LW850, LW900, LW950, LW1000 based on sintering temperature).
